      <content name="title">Family <span class="qt0">History</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your family <span class="qt0">history</span> includes health information about you and your close relatives. Families have many factors in common, including their genes, environment, and lifestyle. Looking at these factors can help you figure out whether you have a higher risk for certain health problems, such as heart disease, stroke, and cancer.</p><p>Having a family member with a disease raises your risk, but it does not mean that you will definitely get it. Knowing that you are at risk gives you a chance to reduce that risk by following a healthier lifestyle and getting tested as needed. </p><p>You can get started by talking to your relatives about their health. Draw a family tree and add the health information. Having copies of medical records and death certificates is also helpful. </p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention </p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/cholesterollevelswhatyouneedtoknow.html">
      <content name="title">Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Familial Combined Hyperlipidemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Familial Dysbetalipoproteinemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Familial Hypercholesterolemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hypercholesterolemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hyperlipidemia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is cholesterol?<p>Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some cholesterol to work properly. But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk of coronary artery disease and other heart diseases.</p>How do you measure cholesterol levels?<p>A blood test called a lipoprotein or lipid panel can measure your cholesterol levels. Before the test, you'll usually need to fast (not eat or drink anything but water) for 9 to 12 hours. Follow the instructions your health care provider gives you.</p><p>The test gives information about your:</p><ul><li>Total cholesterol. This is a measure of the total amount of cholesterol in your blood. It includes both low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol.</li><li>LDL cholesterol. LDL is often called "bad" cholesterol because it is the main source of cholesterol buildup and blockage in the arteries.</li><li>HDL cholesterol. HDL is often called "good" cholesterol because it helps remove cholesterol from your arteries.</li><li>Non-HDL. This number is your total cholesterol minus your HDL. Your non-HDL includes LDL and other types of cholesterol such as VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein). It gives a better picture of all the "bad" types of cholesterol that can raise your heart risk.</li><li>Triglycerides. This is another type of fat in your blood that can raise your risk of heart disease, especially in women.</li></ul>What do my cholesterol numbers mean?<p>Cholesterol numbers are measured in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL). Talk with your provider about what your cholesterol numbers should be. The numbers that are best for you may depend on your age, race, blood pressure, weight, family <span class="qt0">history</span>, and more. However, here are some general guidelines showing the desirable levels (levels that are healthy for most people):</p><p>Anyone age 19 or younger:</p>Type of CholesterolHealthy LevelTotal CholesterolLess than 170 mg/dLNon-HDLLess than 120 mg/dLLDLLess than 110 mg/dLHDLMore than 45mg/dL<p>Men age 20 or older:</p>Type of CholesterolHealthy LevelTotal CholesterolLess than 200 mg/dLNon-HDLLess than 130 mg/dLLDLLess than 100 mg/dLHDLGreater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best.Levels less than 40 mg/dL are considered low.<p>Women age 20 or older:</p>Type of CholesterolHealthy LevelTotal CholesterolLess than 200 mg/dLNon-HDLLess than 130 mg/dLLDLLess than 100 mg/dLHDLGreater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best.Levels less than 50 mg/dL are considered low.<p>Triglycerides are not a type of cholesterol, but they are also measured in this test.  A normal triglyceride level is below 150 mg/dL. You might need treatment if you have triglyceride levels that are borderline high (150-199 mg/dL) or high (200 mg/dL or more).</p>What are risk-based LDL goals?<p>If you have heart disease, or your provider thinks you might be at higher risk, they may use your LDL cholesterol level to help you set goals for your LDL cholesterol levels.</p><p>Your provider may use a new risk estimator tool called PREVENT, which stands for Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs, to guide these goals and estimate your risk of heart disease. It looks at factors like your age, health <span class="qt0">history</span>, and family <span class="qt0">history</span>, and puts you in a risk group.</p><p>LDL goal by risk level</p>Risk levelHealthy LDL LevelLow or borderline risk100 mg/dL or belowHigh risk of future heart attack or stroke70 mg/dL or belowAlready have heart disease70 mg/dL or belowAlready have heart disease and are at very high risk55 mg/dL or belowHow often should I get a cholesterol test?<p>When and how often you should get a cholesterol test depends on your age, risk factors, and family <span class="qt0">history</span>. The general recommendations are:</p><p>For people who are age 21 or younger:</p><ul><li>Children should be screened at least once between ages 9 to 11 and again once between ages 17 and 21</li><li>Some children may have this test starting at age 2 if there is a family <span class="qt0">history</span> of high cholesterol,heart attack, orstroke</li></ul><p>For people who are ages 21 to 65:</p><ul><li>Younger adults should have the test every 5 years</li><li>Men ages 45 to 65 and women ages 55 to 65 should have it every 1 to 2 years</li></ul><p>For people older than 65:</p><ul><li>They should be tested every year</li></ul><p>Additional testing may include:</p><ul><li>A lipoprotein(a) blood test once as an adult, and an apolipoprotein B or "apo B" test if you have certain health conditions. These special blood tests help your provider understand your heart risk.</li><li>A coronary calcium scan may be done to help determine if you need cholesterol medicines. This is animaging testwhich checks to see if you have calcium built up in your heart arteries.</li></ul>What affects my cholesterol levels?<p>Many factors can affect your cholesterol levels. Some of them are things you can change:</p><ul><li>Diet. Saturatedfatand cholesterol in the food you eat make your blood cholesterol level rise. Saturated fat is the main problem, but cholesterol in foods also matters. Reducing the amount of saturated fat in your diet helps lower your blood cholesterol level. Foods that have high levels of saturated fats include red meats, full-fat dairy products, chocolate, some baked goods, and many deep-fried and processed foods.</li><li>Weight. Being overweight or havingobesityare risk factors for heart disease. They also tend to increase your cholesterol. If you have high cholesterol and are overweight, it's recommended that you lose at least 5% of your body weight, which would be 10 pounds for a 200-pound person.</li><li>Lack of physical activity. Not being physically active is a risk factor for heart disease.</li><li>Smoking.Cigarette smokinglowers your HDL cholesterol. Since HDL helps to remove cholesterol from your arteries, having a lower HDL level can contribute to a higher cholesterol level.</li></ul><p>Some factors that you cannot change can also affect your cholesterol levels, such as</p><ul><li>Age. Your cholesterol levels tend to rise as you get older. Even though it is less common, younger people, includingchildren and teens, can also have high cholesterol.</li><li>Sex. Between ages 20 and 39, men have a greater risk of high total cholesterol than women. But aftermenopause, a woman's risk goes up. This happens because menopause lowers levels of female hormones that may protect against high blood cholesterol.</li><li>Family <span class="qt0">history</span>. Your genes partly determine how much cholesterol your body makes. High cholesterol can run in families.</li><li>Ethnicity. Your ethnicity may increase your risk of high cholesterol.</li></ul>How can I lower my cholesterol?<p>You canlower your cholesterolthrough heart-healthy lifestyle changes: They include aheart-healthy eating plan,weight management, andregular physical activity.</p><p>If the lifestyle changes alone do not lower your cholesterol enough, you may also need to take medicines. There are several types ofcholesterol-lowering drugsavailable, includingstatins. You may need a statin if you:</p><ul><li>Are age 30 or older and have an LDL cholesterol of 160 mg/dL or higher</li><li>Have a strong family <span class="qt0">history</span> of heart disease</li></ul><p>If you take medicines to lower your cholesterol, you still should continue with the lifestyle changes.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/heartdiseases.html">
      <content name="title">Heart Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cardiac Diseases</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cardiovascular Diseases</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is heart disease?<p>Heart disease is a general term that includes many types of heart problems. It's a type of cardiovascular disease, which means heart and blood vessel disease.</p><p>Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States, but there are ways to prevent and manage many types of heart disease.</p>What are the types of heart disease?<p>There are many different types of heart disease. Some you may be born with, called congenital heart disease. Other types develop during your lifetime.</p><p>Coronary artery disease (also called coronary heart disease) is the most common type of heart disease. It happens slowly over time when a sticky substance called plaque builds up in the arteries that supply your heart muscle with blood. The plaque narrows or blocks blood flow to the heart muscle and can lead to other heart problems:</p><ul><li>Angina - chest pain from lack of blood flow</li><li>Heart attacks - when part of the heart muscle dies from loss of blood flow</li><li>Heart failure - when your heart can't pump enough blood to meet your body's needs</li><li>Arrhythmia - a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat</li></ul><p>Other types of heart diseases may affect your heart valves or heart muscle (cardiomyopathy).</p>What causes heart diseases?<p>The causes of heart disease depend on the type of disease. Some possible causes include lifestyle, genetics, infections, medicines, and other diseases.</p>Who is more likely to develop heart diseases?<p>There are many different factors that can make you more likely to develop heart disease. Some of these factors you can change, but others you cannot.</p><ul><li>Age. Your risk of heart disease goes up as you get older.</li><li>Sex. Some factors may affect heart disease risk differently in women than in men.</li><li>Family <span class="qt0">history</span> and genetics. A family <span class="qt0">history</span> of early heart disease raises your risk. And research has shown that some genes are linked to a higher risk of certain heart diseases.</li><li>Race/ethnicity. Heart disease is the leading cause of death in most racial and ethnic groups in the United States. However, certain groups have higher risks than others. This includes Black people, White people, and American Indian/Alaska Native people.</li><li>Lifestyle habits. Over time, unhealthy lifestyle habits can raise your risk of heart disease. These can include: 
	<ul><li>Eating a diet high in saturated fats, refined carbohydrates, and salt.</li><li>Not getting enough physical activity.</li><li>Drinking too much alcohol.</li><li>Smoking and exposure to secondhand smoke.</li><li>Too much stress.</li></ul>
</li><li>Having other medical conditions can raise your risk of heart diseases. These conditions include:
	<ul><li>High blood pressure.</li><li>High cholesterol levels.</li><li>Diabetes.</li><li>Obesity.</li><li>Autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.</li><li>Chronic kidney disease.</li><li>Metabolic syndrome.</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the symptoms of heart disease?<p>Your symptoms will depend on the type of heart disease you have. You may not have symptoms at first. In some cases, you may not know you have heart disease until you have a complication such as a heart attack.</p>How are heart diseases diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have heart disease, your health care provider will:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical <span class="qt0">history</span>, including your symptoms</li><li>Ask about your family health <span class="qt0">history</span>, including relatives who have had heart disease</li><li>Do a physical exam</li><li>Likely run heart tests and blood tests</li></ul><p>In some cases, your provider may refer you to a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart diseases) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for heart disease?<p>Treatment plans for heart disease depend on the type of heart disease you have, how serious your symptoms are, and what other health conditions you have. Possible treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Heart-healthy lifestyle changes</li><li>Medicines</li><li>Procedures or surgeries</li><li>Cardiac rehabilitation</li></ul>Can heart diseases be prevented?<p>You may be able to lower your risk of certain heart diseases by making heart-healthy lifestyle changes  and managing any other medical conditions you have.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hemophilia.html">
      <content name="title">Hemophilia</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Blood Coagulation Disorders</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Christmas disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Factor IX deficiency</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Factor VIII deficiency</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is hemophilia?<p>Hemophilia is a rare bleeding disorder in which the blood does not clot properly. This can lead to problems with bleeding too much after an injury or surgery. You can also have sudden bleeding inside your body, such as in your joints, muscles, and organs.</p><p>Your blood contains many proteins called clotting factors that can help form clots to stop bleeding. People with hemophilia have low levels of one of these factors, usually either factor VIII (8) or factor IX (9). How severe the hemophilia is depends on the amount of factor in the blood. The lower the amount of the factor, the more likely it is that bleeding could happen and might lead to serious health problems.</p>What are the types of hemophilia?<p>There are several different types of hemophilia. The most common are:</p><ul><li>Hemophilia A (classic hemophilia), which is caused by a lack or decrease of clotting factor VIII (8)</li><li>Hemophilia B (Christmas disease), which is caused by a lack or decrease of clotting factor IX (9)</li></ul>What causes hemophilia?<p>Most types of hemophilia are inherited. They are caused by change in one of the genes (also called a mutation) that provides instructions for making the clotting factor proteins. The change may mean that the clotting proteins don't work properly or that they are missing altogether.</p><p>These genes are on the X chromosome. You may have one or two X chromosomes:</p><ul><li>People who are born male have one X chromosome (from the mother) and one Y chromosome (from the father). They can get hemophilia if their one X chromosome has the gene change.</li><li>People who are born female have two X chromosomes, one from the father and one from the mother. They usually only get hemophilia if:
	<ul><li>Both X chromosomes have the gene change OR</li><li>One X chromosome has the gene change and the other X chromosome is missing or inactive.</li></ul>
  <p>People who are born female who have the gene change on one X chromosome are a "carrier" of hemophilia. Sometimes they may have some symptoms of hemophilia. They can pass the gene change on to their children.</p>
</li></ul><p>Hemophilia that is not inherited is called acquired hemophilia. It is rare. It happens when your body makes specialized proteins called autoantibodies that attack and disable a clotting factor. This can happen because of pregnancy, immune system disorders, cancer, or allergic reactions to certain medicines. Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p>Who is at risk for hemophilia?<p>Hemophilia is much more common in people who were born male since they can get it with a change to the gene on one X chromosome. People who have a family <span class="qt0">history</span> of hemophilia are also at higher risk.</p>What are the symptoms of hemophilia?<p>The signs and symptoms of hemophilia are:</p><ul><li>Bleeding into the joints. This can cause swelling and pain or tightness in the joints. It often affects the knees, elbows, and ankles.</li><li>Bleeding into the skin (which is bruising).</li><li>Bleeding into the muscle and soft tissue, which can cause a build-up of blood in the area (called a hematoma).</li><li>Bleeding of the mouth and gums, including bleeding that is hard to stop after you lose a tooth.</li><li>Bleeding after circumcision.</li><li>Bleeding after having shots, such as vaccinations.</li><li>Bleeding in the head of an infant after a difficult delivery.</li><li>Blood in the urine or stool.</li><li>Frequent and hard-to-stop nosebleeds.</li></ul><p>In some cases, severe hemophilia may cause bleeding in the brain. This may cause brain damage and can be life-threatening.</p>How is hemophilia diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have hemophilia, your health care provider will:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical <span class="qt0">history</span>, including your symptoms and other health conditions you may have.</li><li>Ask about your family <span class="qt0">history</span>, to find out if you have relatives who have or had hemophilia.</li><li>Do a physical exam to look for signs of hemophilia, such as bruising.</li><li>Do certain blood tests to show if your blood is clotting properly. If it does not, then you will have clotting factor tests to diagnose the cause of the bleeding disorder. These blood tests would show the type of hemophilia and the severity.</li></ul><p>There is genetic testing for the factor VIII (8) and factor IX (9) genes. This testing may be used in people who have a family <span class="qt0">history</span> of hemophilia to:</p><ul><li>Identify people who are carriers before they make decisions about pregnancy</li><li>Test a fetus for hemophilia during pregnancy</li><li>Test a newborn for hemophilia</li></ul>What are the treatments for hemophilia?<p>The best way to treat hemophilia is to replace the missing clotting factor so that your blood can clot properly. This is usually done by injecting replacement clotting factor into a vein. The replacement clotting factor may be made from donated human blood. Or it may be made in a lab; this kind is called a recombinant clotting factor.</p><p>Replacement clotting factor can help treat a bleeding episode. In more severe cases of hemophilia, you might get the factor on a regular basis to prevent bleeding. You can learn how to inject the factor so that you can do it yourself at home.</p><p>There are other medicines to treat hemophilia. They may work by releasing factor VIII (8) from where it is stored in the body tissues, replacing the function of factor VIII (8), or preventing clots from breaking down.</p><p>If bleeding has damaged your joints, physical therapy may help them function better.</p><p>Good quality medical care from healthcare professionals who know a lot about the disorder can help prevent some serious problems. Often the best choice for care is to visit a hemophilia treatment center (HTC).</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ankylosingspondylitis.html">
      <content name="title">Ankylosing Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rheumatoid Spondylitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Spondylitis, Ankylosing</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis of the spine. It causes inflammation (swelling) between your vertebrae (the bones that make up your spine) and the joints between your spine and pelvis. AS inflammation can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend.</p><p>Symptoms of AS can range from mild to severe back pain. Over time, AS can fuse (grow together) your vertebrae, limiting movement and causing a hunched posture. In some people, AS can affect other joints or body parts.</p><p>There is no cure for AS, but early treatment can help manage symptoms, slow down the disease, and help you lead a more productive life.</p>Who is more likely to get ankylosing spondylitis?<p>Ankylosing spondylitis usually starts before age 45. Early symptoms may begin between the ages of 15 and 30. Your chance of developing AS can also increase if:</p><ul><li>You're a man. AS is more common and severe in men.</li><li>You have a family <span class="qt0">history</span>. If a member of your family has AS, you're more likely to get the disease.</li><li>You have other medical conditions that may increase your risk of getting AS. These include Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or psoriasis.</li></ul>What causes ankylosing spondylitis?<p>No one knows what causes ankylosing spondylitis, but the environment and genes likely play a role. Your genes are parts of DNA in your cells that are passed down from your parents. Certain genes may increase your risk of getting the disease, but not everyone with these genes gets AS.</p>What are the symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS affects people differently. The most common symptom is pain and stiffness in the lower back and/or hips. The pain is usually worse during the night or after sitting for a long time.</p><p>Over time, AS may progress to other areas of your spine or body. Symptoms may depend on which areas of your body the disease affects. Some people have symptoms that come and go. Others may have severe, ongoing pain.</p><p>Other symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, stiffness, and inflammation of the joints.</li><li>Difficulty taking a deep breath. This could occur if the joints connecting the ribs are affected.</li><li>Changes in vision.</li><li>Fatigue.</li><li>Loss of appetite.</li><li>Weight loss.</li><li>Skin rashes, such as psoriasis.</li><li>Abdominal (belly) pain and loose stools (poop).</li></ul>How is ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed?<p>There is no single test for ankylosing spondylitis. To find out if you have AS your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical <span class="qt0">history</span>, including your symptoms.</li><li>Ask about your family health <span class="qt0">history</span>, including relatives who have had AS.</li><li>Do a physical exam.</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging studies.</li></ul>What are the treatments for ankylosing spondylitis?<p>AS has no cure, but treatment may help relieve symptoms, maintain posture, and slow down the disease. Since other parts of your body can be affected by AS, you will likely work with a team of health care professionals for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p><p>Treatment usually includes medicine to help relieve symptoms and keep the disease from getting worse, as well as physical therapy to improve mobility. If AS is severe, surgery may be needed.</p><p>You can help manage your AS symptoms if you:</p><ul><li>Exercise</li><li>Monitor your symptoms</li><li>Manage your stress</li><li>Use assistive devices as needed</li><li>Follow a healthy diet</li><li>Stop smoking, or don't start</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Disease</p></content>
